study.title: Psalm 65: God who hears, sustains and makes fruitful
study.overview: This psalm presents God as the only one worthy of praise, because he responds to prayers, forgives guilt, sustains his people and governs creation with power and goodness. The movement of the text goes from worship in Zion to God's action on the whole earth: first in the spiritual life of the people, then in the control of nature and, finally, in the abundant fertility that produces food and joy. The emphasis is that both redemption and providence are reasons for reverence and gratitude.

outline.title: Praise, prayer and access to God's presence
outline.explanation: The psalm begins by stating that God deserves reverent silence, praise and vows fulfilled. He is the God who hears the prayers and to him all mankind must come. It is also the God who removes guilt and grants bliss to those whom he chooses and approaches to live in his home and be satisfied for his goodness.

outline.title: The God of salvation and government on creation
outline.explanation: Here God appears as the one who answers with righteousness and acts that inspire fear. He is the confidence of the ends of the earth, which firms the mountains, calms the sea and controls the turmoil of the peoples. Even those who live far recognize their signs, and the alternation of day and night is also under their dominion.

outline.title: The land visited, watered and crowned with abundance
outline.explanation: The last section describes God as the provider visiting the earth, irrigating and preparing to produce wheat. Rain softens the soil, the year is crowned with kindness and the divine paths overflow. The result is a creation full of herds, wheat fields and sung joy.

study.context: The heading attributes the psalm to David and relates it to the regent, indicating liturgical use. The notes provided treat the psalm as a celebration of the works of God both in redemption and providence. There is no safe data in the notes on specific occasion or concrete historical circumstances.
study.theology: The psalm unites spirituality and creation without separating them. God forgives guilt, receives the people in his presence and satisfies those whom he chooses; this shows the priority of grace. At the same time, he reigns over hills, seas, days, nights, rains and crops, which presents the providence as a continuous expression of his power. The proper human response is praise, reverence, trust and fulfillment of vows. An evangelical Christian reading can see here a picture of the God that saves and sustains, although the text does not detail yet the means of this salvation. The psalm also suggests that the abundance of the earth is not chance, but the Creator's gift, leading the whole creation to a witness of joy.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm shows that praise is the correct answer to the majestic acts of God both in redemption and in nature, and that God takes the blame of sin.
The psalmist presents God's goodness in the kingdom of grace by forgiving sin, satisfying his people and protecting it, before passing into the kingdom of providence.
Fertilizing rains and the abundance produced show God as the one who visits and prepares the earth to support people and animals.

questions: How does our prayer change when we remember that God not only hears, but also forgives and brings his people closer to themselves?
How do we see God's hand in common aspects of life, such as rain, food and seasons of the year?
What does it mean, in practice, to fulfill vows and live with gratitude before a God who governs creation and responds in righteousness?
study.practice: Take a time to praise God for three concrete things: forgiveness received, daily provision, and evidence of his order in creation. Then turn this into a compromise: fulfill a promise made to God, practice gratitude when feeding and pray for people who do not yet recognize their government. Read this psalm aloud as a community or personal prayer, remembering that God's goodness appears in both salvation and daily livelihood.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not allow us to affirm a specific historical occasion for the psalm, nor to safely identify geographical or chronological details behind expressions such as the river of God. Some commented interpretations, such as the reference to the call of the Gentiles, are presented as possibilities and not as a single and obligatory meaning of the text.
